description: The squat is a fundamental lower-body compound movement that trains the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and core. Proper form is critical to protect the knees and lower back. A full squat develops functional strength and mobility that transfers to everyday activities and athletic performance.
cues: Chest proud — imagine someone is about to read your t-shirt
Sit back like there is a chair behind you, don't just bend the knees
Drive your knees out in line with your pinky toes on the way down
Push the floor apart with your feet as you stand
Take a big breath in before you descend and brace your core like you expect a punch
Heels must stay glued to the floor throughout the entire movement
rules: Keep chest up and back straight throughout the movement
Push hips back before bending knees
Keep knees aligned with second and third toes
Lower until thighs are at least parallel to the ground
Drive through full foot to return to standing
constraints: Do not let knees collapse inward (valgus collapse)
Do not lift heels off the ground
Avoid excessive forward lean of the torso
Do not perform partial squats — reach parallel or below
Avoid using momentum — each rep should be controlled
Maintain left-right symmetry through the entire movement

knees_caving_in.cause: Weak hip abductors and glutes, or placing feet too narrow.
knees_caving_in.consequence: Excessive medial knee stress leading to patellofemoral pain and long-term ligament damage (ACL/MCL).
knees_caving_in.fix: Actively push your knees out in the direction of your pinky toes. Strengthen glute medius with resistance band walks before squatting.

heels_lifting.cause: Limited ankle dorsiflexion mobility or weight shifted too far forward.
heels_lifting.consequence: Shifts load from glutes to lower back; destabilises the lift entirely.
heels_lifting.fix: Work on ankle mobility stretches daily. Temporarily elevate heels on a small plate to allow full depth until flexibility improves.

forward_lean.cause: Tight hip flexors or thoracic spine stiffness causing the torso to fold forward.
forward_lean.consequence: Transfers load to the lumbar spine — a major cause of lower back injury.
forward_lean.fix: Keep your chest up by imagining someone is pulling your sternum toward the ceiling. Open up with thoracic rotations before your session.

shallow_squat.cause: Insufficient hip and ankle mobility, or trying to use more weight than current mobility allows.
shallow_squat.consequence: Reduces glute activation and training stimulus; also trains a limited range of motion.
shallow_squat.fix: Aim for thighs at least parallel. Box squats to a target depth are a great training tool.

using_momentum.cause: Bouncing at the bottom of the squat or rushing the descent.
using_momentum.consequence: Reduces time under tension, offloads the muscles, and adds dangerous stress to the knee joint.
using_momentum.fix: Slow the descent to 2–3 seconds, pause briefly at the bottom, then drive up with intention.

uneven_weight.cause: Muscle imbalances between left and right side, or asymmetric foot placement.
uneven_weight.consequence: Over-stresses one joint and creates compensatory patterns that lead to injury.
uneven_weight.fix: Film yourself from the front and identify which side drops. Single-leg exercises like split squats help correct the weaker side.

tilt.note: Forward tilt of torso — keep below 20 degrees

acceleration.note: Spike indicates momentum; smooth acceleration preferred

stability.note: Composite balance score from MPU6050 variance

symmetry.note: Left-right acceleration symmetry from dual sensor setup
